title: Calcium imaging of adult-born neurons in freely moving mice
protocol: Prepare a 20 mg/mL tamoxifen solution.
Heat corn oil to 42°C for 30 minutes.
Dissolve tamoxifen in corn oil at a concentration of 20 mg/mL using an ultrasonic bath or continuous shaking at 37°C.
Store the prepared tamoxifen solution at 4°C away from light.
Select adult nestin:GCaMP3 mice based on sexual maturity (typically ∼6 weeks of age).
Administer tamoxifen (120 mg/kg) into the intraperitoneal cavity five times at 1- or 2-day intervals.
Store the tamoxifen solution at 4°C until the next injection.
Wait a pre-determined period after tamoxifen injection for GCaMP3-labeled ABNs to mature before proceeding to the next step.
Surgically implant a gradient-index (GRIN) lens into the brains of tamoxifen-injected mice.
Implant electroencephalogram (EEG)/electromyogram (EMG) electrodes into the brains of tamoxifen-injected mice.
Anesthetize the mouse with an anesthetic of choice (e.g., isoflurane).
Shave hair from the surgical site.
Open a cranial window sufficiently large for lens and electrode implantation.
Secure the head of the mouse in a stereotaxic frame.
Cover the eyes of the mouse with white petrolatum cream to prevent dryness.
Disinfect the skin at the surgical site.
Make a small incision in the skin using a spring scissor along the sagittal line of the skull.
Clean the exposed skull with cotton swabs.
Scratch the skull surface using a drill bit to make it rough.
Obtain a flat skull position by matching the height of two parallel points along the sagittal axis (±3 mm lateral from bregma) as well as the height of bregma and lambda points.
Mark the desired stereotaxic coordinates for the GRIN lens and EEG electrodes on the skull surface using the stereotaxic manipulator.
Drill one hole in the skull for the GRIN lens.
Drill two holes over one hemisphere for EEG electrodes.
Drill two holes over the contralateral hemisphere for anchoring electrodes.
Make a cranial window for GRIN lens implantation using a drill.
Aspirate cortical tissue above the region of interest using a glass pipette connected to a vacuum pump in circular movements from the center to the periphery of the cranial window.
Stop aspiration when white matter tracts of the corpus callosum and alveus hippocampus are visible as identified by striations.
Irrigate exposed brain tissue continuously with sterile saline while aspirating cortical tissue.
Keep the exposed brain tissue irrigated with sterile saline during aspiration of blood present in the region to maintain visibility.
Carefully lower the GRIN lens using 0.1-mm dorso-ventral steps into the hippocampus.
Fix the GRIN lens to the skull and all four screws with a thin layer of cyanoacrylate adhesive (Loctite 454).
Allow the glue to cure for approximately 5–10 minutes.
Release the lens from the stereotaxic manipulator.
Cover the skull using a layer of Loctite glue and dental cement liquid around the insertion point.
Attach the EEG/EMG socket to the skull using Loctite glue, add a drop of dental cement liquid, and allow it to completely cure.
Insert two wires into the cervical portion of the trapezoid muscles for EMG recording.
Apply carbon black powder-mixed dental cement (liquid + powder) to any exposed area of the skull as well as to the area where the Loctite glue meets the GRIN lens and EEG/EMG wires.
Cover the EEG/EMG wires with Loctite glue to prevent damage when the mouse scratches its head.
Apply Loctite glue to the outer border of the dental cement to connect it to the surrounding skin and wait until it completely cures.
Cover the GRIN lens and surrounding area with silicone to protect it from damage resulting from mouse activity in the home cage.
Attach a rectangular metal frame (12 × 19 × 1 mm) to the skull using dental cement and let it solidify for 5 min.
Stop anesthesia.
Remove the mouse from the stereotaxic holder.
Administer postoperative 5% glucose solution and ibuprofen (30 mg/kg).
Place the mouse in a clean cage partially covering a heating pad to prevent hypothermia and allow it to recover.
House the operated mouse individually to avoid damage to the implant.
Allow operated mice to rest for at least 1 week with minimal manipulation.
Anesthetize the mouse with an anesthetic of choice (e.g., isoflurane).
Secure the head of the mouse in the stereotaxic frame.
Prepare the miniscope.
Attach the magnetic baseplate to the miniscope.
Secure the miniscope to its gripper tool and attach it to a micromanipulator.
Connect the recording hardware to the computer.
Position the miniscope above the head of the mouse.
Start the image acquisition software.
Attach the magnetic baseplate.
Remove the silicone protection from the skull of the mouse.
Adjust the position of the miniscope using the micromanipulator, centering it above the implanted lens.
Turn on the LED light of the miniscope and lower it until the top surface of the lens becomes visible through the camera.
Carefully continue lowering the miniscope until the DG becomes visible.
Lower the miniscope ∼50 μm to adjust the imaging focus to the granular/subgranular layer.
Switch to the nVista software ΔF/F function to confirm the presence of dynamic changes in fluorescence corresponding to Ca2+ transients.
Secure the baseplate to the skull using dental cement, ensuring there are no gaps around the implanted lens, screw for the magnetic baseplate, and miniscope.
Finish the imaging preparation.
Release the miniscope from the gripper tool after the dental cement has solidified completely.
Detach the miniscope from the magnetic baseplate, which remains attached to the skull.
Attach the baseplate cover to prevent dust on the lens.
Release the mouse and return it to its home cage.
Habituate mice to the miniscope and EEG/EMG cables by attaching dummy devices.
Hold the mouse head gently on both sides of the implant during habituation.
Remove the baseplate cover and attach the dummy miniscope and dummy EEG/EMG cables.
Place the mouse inside the sleeping chamber for approximately 6 hours.
Visually confirm periodically whether the mouse is sleeping.
Repeat the habituation protocol on the following day until the mouse can sleep and move freely in the sleeping chamber.
Remove the dummy materials after completion of the habituation session.
Attach the baseplate cover back onto the setup.
Return the mouse to its home cage.
Record EEG/EMG and Ca2+ transients during sleep.
Prepare the mouse for EEG/EMG recording and Ca2+ imaging.
Start the acquisition software and set the imaging parameters.
Secure the miniscope and EEG/EMG cables above the recording chamber.
Place the EEG/EMG and miniscope cable close to each other so that their rotation axes are similar.
Monitor the state of the mouse and cables periodically during recording period.
Start EEG/EMG recording and Ca2+ imaging simultaneously.
Fear condition mice with tones and foot shocks.
Prepare the mouse for the fear conditioning chamber.
Remove the baseplate cover and attach the miniscope.
Start the Ca2+ imaging acquisition software and set the imaging parameters.
Arrange the cables above the conditioning chamber using the same precautions as for the sleeping chamber.
Use the dummy miniscope if the actual recording equipment is not needed during conditioning.
Place the mouse inside the conditioning chamber.
Perform Ca2+ imaging for 10 minutes during the pre-conditioning period (pre-shock recording).
Stop the imaging and quickly detach the miniscope, then reattach the dummy miniscope in less than 1 minute to avoid changes due to shock or field of view alteration.
Quickly reattach the miniscope and perform 5 minutes of Ca2+ imaging (post-shock recording).
Finish the recording and return the mouse to the sleeping chamber.
Connect the EEG/EMG cable.
Start simultaneous EEG/EMG recording and Ca2+ imaging.
Record EEG/EMG activity and Ca2+ transients.
Transfer the sleeping chamber to the sleep recording room.
Cover the interior walls of the conditioning chamber with shock-absorbing material if necessary.
Avoid detaching the miniscope and cables from the head of the mouse when transferring it to the sleeping chamber.
Disconnect the cables from the computer port if necessary before transferring the mouse.
Reconnect the cables after transferring the mouse if they were disconnected.
Confirm whether freezing is specifically observed in the shocked context for properly habituated mice.
Prepare the mouse for the fear conditioning chamber as done on previous days.
Start the EEG/EMG recording and Ca2+ imaging simultaneously.
Use the dummy miniscope if not recording is needed during conditioning.
Confirm the establishment of a fear memory.
Start EEG/EMG recording and Ca2+ imaging software.
Place the mouse inside the conditioning chamber.
Start the EEG/EMG recording and Ca2+ imaging simultaneously.
Leave the mouse inside the chamber for 5–10 min.
Euthanize the mouse according to institutional guidelines.
Transcardially perfuse the mouse with cold 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA).
Remove the brain and place it inside a tube with 4% PFA at 4°C for 24 h.
Pause the experiment.
Exchange PFA for phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) after 24 hours and protect the tube from light.
Replace 4% PFA with 20%-30% sucrose solution if using a cryostat for slicing.
Remove the brain from the tube after it sinks.
Cryopreserve the brain in an OCT mounting medium block at -80°C.
Slice the brain at 50 μm thickness using a cryostat or vibratome.
Collect brain slices in plastic wells or dishes with desired buffer.
Add 0.1% sodium azide to the buffer if storing slices at 4°C for bacterial prevention.
Confirm the location of the implanted lens and GCaMP3 fluorescence signal on brain slices.
Mount brain slices on microscope slides using fluorescence-preserving medium.
Image the mounted slides with a fluorescence microscope.
